# Verification\chaptersubtitle{Breaking the Assembled Machine to See If Its Claims Hold} {#sec-verification}

![**Systems Organ Focus: Nervous.** The fault list derived from the records, as a traceable mapping](figures/fig_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch15 fig-pos="H" width=100%}

*Do the claims this machine rests on survive a deliberate attack on each one?*

A physical machine cannot be certified safe by running thousands of unperturbed operational hours under nominal conditions. Standard fleet testing exercises only common scenarios, leaving catastrophic corner cases and hidden failure modes entirely unprobed. Whole-system verification is the adversarial engineering discipline of subjecting the integrated machine to systematic, deterministic fault injection across every stage of the qualification ladder. By deliberately corrupting memory buffers, dropping sensor packets, inducing brownouts, and locking actuator shafts on test benches, engineers measure the exact physical boundaries of the survival envelope and falsify safety claims before hardware is released into unconstrained operational environments.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-objective}
After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

1. State an operating envelope precisely enough that a condition outside it can be deliberately created.
2. Derive a fault list by walking the records from Chapters 5 to 14 and violating each stated property.
3. Inject a stale observation, a late plan, and an expired intent on real hardware, and record what happened.
4. Say what a given rung of the qualification ladder can establish and what it cannot.

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** The fault list is derived from what the design claims, not chosen from a menu of techniques. Every property recorded in Parts II and III is a fault waiting to be injected, and the intervention mechanism is under test alongside everything else.

:::

## Introduction {#sec-verification-15-1}

<!-- SECTION 15.1 -->
<!-- claim: A machine that worked in front of you is not evidence that it works, and this chapter is about what would be. -->
<!-- covers: Open on a machine that has run successfully for weeks, and separate the existence claim one successful run establishes from the reliability, envelope, and fault-tolerance claims it cannot. -->
<!-- covers: Show that a nominal success rate is conditional on the sampled operating distribution and says nothing about excluded boundaries, rare faults, or correlated disturbances. -->
<!-- covers: Trace a flow regulator that succeeds repeatedly at nominal pressure and has never encountered a delayed level observation near the overflow boundary. -->
<!-- covers: Name the ingredients that turn a run into evidence: a bounded claim, defined test conditions, a precommitted oracle, a stated sampling or injection procedure, and provenance. The chapter builds each in turn. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: failure — what a working demonstration establishes, and what it does not -->
<!-- DERIVE: why a successful trajectory cannot support a claim over unobserved conditions -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A flow controller that has operated inside an industrial facility for three weeks without an operator intervention has demonstrated exactly one property. It has proven that there exists at least one sequence of benign physical states, undisturbed sensor readings, and nominal actuator commands under which the policy stabilizes the liquid level. This is an existence proof, and an existence proof cannot establish a reliability metric, an operating envelope, or a guarantee of fault tolerance. A machine that worked in front of an observer is not evidence that it works, because an uninstrumented demonstration records only a sample from an uncharacterized, narrow slice of reality. If the ambient temperature remained within $20.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $24.0^\circ\text{C}$, the supply pressure stayed at $3.0\text{ bar}$, and the upstream pump never cavitated, the test stand did not evaluate the controller. It evaluated the benign operating environment.

As mapped in the four-tier architectural locator (@fig-locator-ch15), whole-system verification sits in the nervous system tier as the adversarial auditor of the entire stack. Every design property established across the Body (mechanical inertia, thermal dissipation, actuator slew limits), the Brain (training distribution bounds, inference latencies, intent validity windows), and the Nervous System (bus arbitration, clock synchronization, safety enforcers, authority transfer) is not a permanent truth, but an explicit claim that must be attacked. The fault list is not selected arbitrarily from a generic menu of techniques; it is derived directly by inverting the architectural records and physical constraints of the assembled machine.

The mathematical reason a successful trajectory cannot support a claim over unobserved conditions rests on distribution support. Consider an analytical example where a machine executes $n = 10^6$ control cycles at $100\text{ Hz}$, corresponding to $2.8\text{ hours}$ of continuous operation, with zero observed violations of its state constraints. Under a stationary operational distribution $D_0$, this sequence establishes an empirical failure rate of zero, allowing an engineer to place a statistical upper bound on the per-cycle failure probability on $D_0$. But physical environments are neither stationary nor confined to the center of their probability distributions. The true operating environment $D$ includes rare supply surges, sensor degradation, and thermal drift whose joint probability mass lies in the tail region $D \setminus D_0$. Because the empirical evaluation collected zero samples in this region, the observed data provides zero information about the policy gradient, the actuator saturation limits, or the numerical stability of the state estimator when forced outside $D_0$. A neural network policy that maps state observations to valve positions is an unconstrained function outside the convex hull of its training and testing trajectories. Its output on an unvisited state is not merely uncertain; it is arbitrary.

Consider a flow regulator designed to maintain liquid in a $100.0\text{ L}$ buffer tank below an overflow weir at $95.0\text{ L}$. Under nominal conditions, liquid enters at $40.0\text{ L/min}$, an ultrasound sensor reports the liquid height with a $10\text{ ms}$ bus latency, and an electric actuator adjusts the discharge valve at $50\text{ Hz}$. In routine operation, the liquid height hovers at $60.0\text{ L}$, well clear of the boundary. The machine appears successful because the disturbances never exceed $\pm 5.0\text{ L/min}$, and the discharge valve operates within its linear flow regime between $30\%$ and $50\%$ open. Now introduce an unobserved condition where an upstream valve switch causes a supply pressure spike, driving the inlet flow to $80.0\text{ L/min}$. Simultaneously, a memory bus conflict on the controller board delays the ultrasound reading by $140\text{ ms}$, bringing the total sensing latency to $150\text{ ms}$. With a net fill rate of $40.0\text{ L/min}$, which is $0.67\text{ L/s}$, the tank accumulates volume rapidly. Because the policy receives delayed level data, it underestimates the rate of rise near $90.0\text{ L}$ and commands the discharge valve to open late. When the stale reading finally updates, the policy outputs a maximum-rate slew command that slams the valve open, inducing a hydraulic pressure transient of $12.0\text{ bar}$ that cracks the downstream pipe coupling. The liquid breaches the $95.0\text{ L}$ weir, triggering an emergency float switch that cuts pump power, but the structural damage to the pipe fitting is detected by no runtime sensor at all until fluid pools on the floor.

Converting an execution trace into verification evidence requires structured methods designed to challenge specific system properties. Five ingredients turn a physical run into a test result that can support a safety case. First is a bounded claim, which states the exact invariant the machine must maintain, such as keeping the liquid volume below $95.0\text{ L}$ and the transient line pressure below $6.0\text{ bar}$. Second are defined test conditions, specifying the initial state space, fluid viscosity, ambient temperature, and supply pressure range. Third is a precommitted oracle, an automated evaluator that inspects the recorded telemetry against the claim without human intervention or post-hoc adjustments. Fourth is a stated sampling or injection procedure that deliberately drives the machine toward its performance limits and injects faults into its sensors, buses, and actuators. Fifth is provenance, the complete metadata record of model weights, calibration tables, sensor serial numbers, and raw sensor logs that permits an external engineer to reconstruct the execution and reproduce the result.

Without these five elements, a thousand hours of spotless test stand operation provide no evidentiary value. A machine that worked in front of you is not evidence that it works; it is only evidence that it has not yet encountered the combination of state, disturbance, and latency that breaks it. To construct evidence that satisfies a safety argument, the engineering task shifts from observing nominal behavior to systematically constructing tests that attempt to violate every design claim. That construction begins with the formal boundary that separates the conditions where the machine is guaranteed to perform from the conditions where it is permitted to fail.
<!-- END -->

## The Operating Envelope {#sec-verification-15-2}

<!-- SECTION 15.2 -->
<!-- claim: The conditions under which the machine is claimed to work, stated precisely enough to be violated on purpose. -->
<!-- covers: Express the envelope as measurable ranges and combinations for physical state, environment, sensing quality, timing, compute load, power, and human availability. -->
<!-- covers: Distinguish the claimed operating envelope from the larger survival envelope within which enforcement must still bring the machine to a bounded state. -->
<!-- covers: Derive the remaining reaction time of a pumped reservoir from usable volume margin divided by worst-case net inflow. -->
<!-- covers: Show why independent minimum-and-maximum tables are insufficient when pressure, viscosity, valve response, and observation age interact. -->
<!-- covers: Require every boundary to have units, measurement provenance, uncertainty, and an accountable owner who can accept or narrow the claim. -->
<!-- covers: Select test points on, just inside, and just outside each consequential boundary rather than testing only nominal interior points. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: mechanism — the operating envelope stated precisely enough to violate on purpose -->
<!-- FIGURE: a boundary plot showing where the claimed operating envelope, survival envelope, and deliberately violated conditions separate -->
<!-- DERIVE: the flow regulator’s time-to-limit boundary from conservation of volume rather than asserting a permissible delay -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
The **operating envelope** defines the complete set of simultaneous physical states, environmental disturbances, sensing conditions, execution latencies, compute loads, electrical supply variations, and operator response times under which the machine is claimed to satisfy its performance specifications. Stating this envelope is not an exercise in cataloging typical operating points. Instead, the boundary must be defined with enough numerical precision that an automated test framework can drive the system past each edge on purpose. For a fluid regulation system, this means specifying not merely a nominal liquid level, but the exact allowable ranges for fluid temperature, kinematic viscosity, supply line pressure fluctuations, ambient temperature, acoustic transducer signal-to-noise ratios, CAN bus arbitration jitter, CPU thermal throttling states, supply rail voltage droop, and the maximum permissible time before an operator acknowledges an alert.

An operating envelope is distinct from the larger **survival envelope** that encompasses it. Inside the operating envelope, the learned policy and primary tracking controllers have full authority to regulate the physical process, maintaining closed-loop tracking within tight error tolerances. When external disturbances, sensor failures, or compute stalls push the system across the boundary of the operating envelope, nominal regulation is conceded. At that threshold, the machine enters the survival envelope, where the primary objective shifts entirely to bringing the physical body to a bounded, safe state before structural limits are breached. In the flow regulator, the survival envelope defines the broader region of volume, pressure, and temperature within which emergency shutoff valves and mechanical relief mechanisms can successfully vent pressure and arrest inflow before a pipe ruptures or fluid overflows secondary containment. Beyond the boundary of the survival envelope lies catastrophic physical failure, where stored energy or incoming mass exceeds the mechanical dissipation capacity of the hardware.

Defining the boundary of the operating envelope requires deriving physical limits from first principles rather than asserting convenient software timeouts. Consider a pumped reservoir with an overflow weir at $V_{\text{max}} = 95.0\text{ L}$ and a nominal operating target of $80.0\text{ L}$. When the system operates at an instantaneous volume of $V(t) = 90.0\text{ L}$, the remaining volume margin is $\Delta V = V_{\text{max}} - V(t) = 5.0\text{ L}$. If the supply pump delivers a maximum inflow of $Q_{\text{in}} = 1.25\text{ L/s}$ while a downstream valve failure drops discharge to $Q_{\text{out}} = 0.0\text{ L/s}$, conservation of volume dictates a net accumulation rate of $dV/dt = Q_{\text{in}} - Q_{\text{out}} = 1.25\text{ L/s}$. The remaining reaction time before liquid breaches the weir is $t_{\text{react}} = \Delta V / (dV/dt) = 5.0\text{ L} / (1.25\text{ L/s}) = 4.00\text{ s}$. Every source of delay in the machine consumes a fraction of this four-second budget. If an emergency isolation valve requires $1.00\text{ s}$ of mechanical transit time to seat against line pressure, and fluid acoustic settling consumes $0.20\text{ s}$, the combined budget for sensing delay, inference execution, bus transport, and safety enforcer evaluation cannot exceed $2.80\text{ s}$ at $P_{99.9}$. If the instantaneous volume rises to $V(t) = 93.0\text{ L}$, the remaining volume margin shrinks to $2.0\text{ L}$, and the total reaction time drops to $1.60\text{ s}$. Subtracting the same $1.20\text{ s}$ of mechanical and hydraulic response leaves a total computation and communication budget of only $0.40\text{ s}$ before an unmitigated overflow becomes physically inevitable.

Tabulating separate minimum and maximum values for individual variables fails to capture the true operating boundary because physical and computational dimensions are coupled. In isolation, an inlet pressure of $6.0\text{ bar}$, a fluid viscosity of $45.0\text{ mPa}\cdot\text{s}$, a valve slew rate of $30.0\text{ deg/s}$, and an observation age of $120\text{ ms}$ might each fall within their respective single-variable ranges. When these conditions coincide, the higher viscosity increases fluid shear across the valve spool, slowing mechanical travel below the nominal slew rate. Simultaneously, the elevated inlet pressure accelerates volume accumulation, while the $120\text{ ms}$ observation age hides the initial pressure surge from the policy. The physical state crosses into the survival envelope long before any single parameter exceeds its isolated maximum. The true operating boundary is an interconnected hypersurface in state, parameter, and latency space. A valid verification suite must probe this combined surface rather than checking isolated scalar limits.

To prevent envelope boundaries from deteriorating into optimistic assumptions, every defined parameter must specify its physical units, its measurement provenance, its calibrated uncertainty, and a designated subsystem engineer who remains accountable for its validity. A boundary stated as a maximum pressure of $8.0\text{ bar}$ is incomplete without recording whether that limit derives from hydrostatic burst testing of the flanged joints, finite-element pipe stress models, or pump stall characteristics. The boundary specification must include the measurement uncertainty of the sensors used during characterization, such as $\pm 0.15\text{ bar}$ at $P_{99}$, and must name the individual engineer authorized to accept or narrow the claim. When system components change, such as swapping an elastomeric seal or upgrading a CAN transceiver, the designated owner must formally re-evaluate whether the physical boundary has shifted.

Verification of the operating envelope requires a disciplined sampling strategy that deliberately attacks the boundary surface. Testing nominal interior points, where the tank sits at $50.0\text{ L}$, ambient temperature is $21.0^\circ\text{C}$, and sensing latency is $12\text{ ms}$, demonstrates only that the machine functions under ideal conditions. To generate rigorous verification evidence, the test framework must place test points directly on, immediately inside, and immediately outside each consequential boundary. Evaluating points just inside the boundary verifies that the policy maintains closed-loop stability under maximum permissible stress. Evaluating points on the boundary confirms that safety margins do not collapse under nominal sensor noise. Evaluating points just outside the boundary confirms that safety enforcers intervene predictably, taking authority from the learned policy and bringing the system to a safe halt within the survival envelope before containment is lost.

Formally documenting the operating and survival boundaries converts the design claims of the preceding chapters into concrete targets for fault injection. When every physical constraint, latency budget, and environmental limit is stated as a verifiable number, the safety engineer knows precisely what conditions the machine must withstand, what thresholds must trigger protective intervention, and what dynamic claims must be subjected to deliberate failure.
<!-- END -->

## Deriving the Fault List {#sec-verification-15-3}
